Chapter 6
Concerning New Principalities Which Are Acquired By One's Own Arms And Ability

Do not be surprised if I use the highest examples of leaders and states when discussing entirely new principalities. People almost always walk in paths beaten by others and imitate their deeds. But they can never perfectly follow another's path or match the exact power of those they imitate. A wise leader should always follow the paths of great men and imitate those who have achieved supremacy. That way, even if your ability falls short, it will at least carry a hint of their greatness. Act like a clever archer. When an archer wants to hit a distant target and knows the limits of their bow, they aim much higher than the mark. They do not do this to shoot their arrow into the sky, but to use that high aim to hit the target they actually want to reach.

In entirely new principalities with a new prince, the difficulty of holding onto power depends entirely on the prince's ability, or Virtù. Rising from a private citizen to a prince requires either exceptional ability or good luck, known as Fortuna. Naturally, having one or the other will help smooth over many difficulties. However, the ruler who relies least on luck will hold his power the longest and strongest. It also makes things easier when the prince has no other territories and is forced to live in the new state in person.

Let us look at those who became princes through their own ability and not through luck. Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, and Theseus are the most excellent examples. You could argue we should not discuss Moses, since he was simply executing the will of God. Still, he deserves admiration just for the grace that made him worthy to speak with God. But if you look at Cyrus and others who acquired or founded kingdoms, they are all extraordinary. When you examine their specific actions and methods, they are no less impressive than Moses, even though Moses had God as his teacher. When you study their lives and deeds, you will see they owed nothing to luck except opportunity. Opportunity simply gave them the raw material to shape into whatever form they saw fit. Without that opportunity, their brilliant minds would have gone to waste. But without their brilliance, the opportunity would have been completely useless.

Therefore, it was necessary for Moses to find the Israelites enslaved and oppressed in Egypt. Only in that desperate state were they willing to follow him out of bondage. It was necessary for Romulus to be exiled from Alba and abandoned at birth. That hardship was required for him to become the King of Rome and the founder of his homeland. It was necessary for Cyrus to find the Persians angry with the rule of the Medes, and to find the Medes soft and weak from a long peace. Theseus could not have proven his greatness if he had not found the Athenians scattered and divided. These opportunities gave these men their lucky breaks. But it was their exceptional ability that allowed them to recognize those opportunities, which ultimately brought glory and fame to their countries.

Men who become princes through their own strength and ability face immense difficulty in acquiring their states, but they hold onto them easily. The difficulties of taking power come partly from the new rules and methods they are forced to introduce to secure their new government. Remember this: there is nothing more difficult to plan, more dangerous to execute, or more likely to fail than creating a new system of government. The innovator makes enemies of everyone who thrived under the old system. Meanwhile, he only gets lukewarm support from those who might benefit under the new one. This weak support comes partly from their fear of the enemies, who still have the old laws on their side. But it also comes from human skepticism. People do not truly believe in new things until they have seen them work over a long period of time. Because of this, whenever the prince's enemies have a chance to attack, they do so with fierce partisan passion. Meanwhile, his supporters defend him half-heartedly, placing the prince and his new regime in serious danger.

To fully understand this, we must ask if these innovators stand on their own or if they depend on others. Specifically, to achieve their goals, do they have to beg for help, or can they use force? If they have to rely on begging and prayers, they always fail and accomplish nothing. But when they can rely on themselves and use force, they are rarely in danger. This is why all armed prophets have conquered, and all unarmed prophets have been destroyed. Beyond what I have already said, the nature of people is deeply fickle. It is easy to persuade a crowd of something, but it is extremely difficult to keep them convinced. Therefore, a leader must be ready. When the people stop believing, you must be able to force them to believe.

If Moses, Cyrus, Theseus, and Romulus had been unarmed, they could never have enforced their laws for long. Just look at what happened in our own time to Fra Girolamo Savonarola. His new system of government collapsed the moment the public lost faith in him. Because he was unarmed, he had no way to keep his supporters loyal or to force the unbelievers to obey. Men like this face massive obstacles in achieving their goals. All their true dangers are in the climb to power, and they can only overcome them with immense ability. But once they conquer those obstacles and eliminate the rivals who envied them, they earn deep respect. From that point on, they remain powerful, secure, honored, and happy.

To these great examples, I want to add a lesser one. It still shares the same traits, and it will serve as the final example for this kind of leader: Hiero of Syracuse. Hiero rose from a private citizen to become the Prince of Syracuse. Like the others, he owed nothing to luck except opportunity. The people of Syracuse were oppressed, so they chose him as their military captain. From there, he proved himself and was made their prince. Even as a private citizen, his ability was so immense that writers said he lacked nothing to be a king except a kingdom. Once in power, he abolished the old military and built a new one. He dropped old alliances and forged new ones. Because he built his own loyal army and his own network of allies, he laid a foundation strong enough to support any empire. Hiero endured massive struggles to gain his power, but he had very little trouble keeping it.
Hiero the Second lived from about 307 B.C. to 216 B.C.
